This increasing angle leads to peak torque at 90 degrees, decreasing torque beyond that, and ultimately negative torque (braking) when the angle exceeds 180 degrees.  Negative torque causes the rotor to stall. In a stable system, the stator and rotor frequencies must be equal, so the torque angle remains constant; any deviation initiates continuous angle rotation and eventual stalling.
>
>
> At 300 RPM, the system was stable because the target and actual speeds matched, resulting in zero speed difference and no governor action. During acceleration to 450 RPM, the governor forced the stator frequency to exceed the rotor's physical capability due to the eddy brake, leading to continuous torque angle slip. This frequency difference causes the torque angle to slip, resulting in negative torque and eventual rotor stall after a few seconds.
>
>
> A synchronous machine requires closed-loop control, with stator frequency tracking rotor speed based on encoder feedback to maintain synchronicity. Torque in a PMSM is determined by stator voltage magnitude and the stator field acceleration rate. The torque angle, fundamental to synchronous machine operation, is determined by the ratio of load torque to maximum available torque. With sufficient stator voltage, the maximum torque is high, maintaining a small torque angle.
>
>
> Adding a constant frequency offset to the stator creates continuous phase slip, preventing synchronism between stator and rotor, which is the operational principle of an induction motor, not a synchronous BLDC motor. A BLDC motor requires the average stator and rotor frequencies to be identical for synchronous operation. The optical governor serves to prevent this slip. If the stator speed increases and the rotor accelerates with it, the governor's role becomes crucial.
>
>
> The governor clamps the commanded speed when the difference between commanded and actual speed exceeds a threshold, preventing runaway stator speed and allowing the rotor to catch up. Increasing voltage is the correct action when the commanded speed is greater than the actual rotor speed. A low voltage (5.41V) resulted in insufficient current (70 mA) at 304 RPM, failing to accelerate the rotor toward the 450 RPM target. The required voltage to achieve a target current can be calculated, taking into account resistance and back-EMF.
>
>
> A voltage calculation, based on the difference between the applied voltage and back-EMF, indicated a current much higher than the measured 70 mA. The stator frequency slipping relative to the rotor explained the discrepancy, causing the torque angle to rotate continuously. Data confirmed that the current in the rotor frame ($I_q$) exhibited a clear AC oscillation, averaging near zero, due to the slip frequency.
>
>
> The current in the rotor frame ($I_q$) oscillates, indicating that the stator and rotor frequencies are not synchronized due to a positive `target_lead` value, which forces the stator frequency to be faster than the rotor. This frequency difference causes an electrical slip of 0.355 Hz. The torque angle completes a full rotation every 2.82 seconds, resulting in alternating motoring and braking torque over each cycle, with zero average torque. The rotor is unable to accelerate and eventually stalls because the eddy current brake combines with negative torque during the slip cycle.
>
>
> A permanent magnet synchronous motor requires the stator and rotor frequencies to match for steady-state operation; any frequency slip prevents stable motoring. Open-loop control, commanding a speed ramp, works if the rotor can synchronously track the rotating field. A heavy load, however, causes the rotor speed to lag, resulting in increasing frequency and angle error. If the commanded speed continues to ramp up, the error grows without bound.
>
>
> The optical governor needs to be a closed-loop slip limiter, ensuring the commanded stator speed never significantly outpaces the rotor speed. The goal is to keep the stator and rotor frequencies nearly equal to minimize slip and maintain a stable torque angle. The projected rotor speed is calculated between optical pulses and used to limit the stator speed. The acceleration rate of the projected speed and the command ramp is what accelerates the motor.
>
>
> Voltage increase is needed to overcome the eddy brake's load at various RPMs. Examining the voltage equation shows several contributing factors to target voltage, including a boost term, back-EMF, and load compensation. The `V_target` calculation needs to be understood.
>
>
> The low target voltage at 304 RPM was due to a relatively small eddy current voltage drop, computed using a specific damping coefficient. Increasing this damping coefficient significantly raises the eddy current voltage at 300 and 450 RPM, thus increasing the total `v_target`. With the increased eddy current voltage, and an assumed increase in current, the system should produce sufficient motoring torque at 450 RPM to overcome the eddy brake.
>
>
> A zero or clamped `target_lead` should ensure precise tracking of the projected RPM, resulting in zero slip and a constant torque angle. The stator and rotor angular frequencies would be equal, with $I_q$ remaining as a pure positive DC value. The optical governor still provides safety by limiting speed error. Testing this involves setting `target_lead` to 0.2 RPM in motor control and adjusting the eddy damping coefficient in the motor profiles. The 0.2 RPM lead introduces negligible phase drift, maintaining synchronism. Damping is adjusted to analyze eddy current effects.

>
>
> The motor enters a slip cycle when the commanded stator frequency exceeds the rotor frequency, causing the torque angle to rotate. This leads to alternating motoring and regenerative braking phases. Examining a previous run confirms this, showing oscillatory Iq current, indicating a slip cycle where the motor attempts to self-brake due to a frequency lead. The root cause appears to be the ramped speed command exceeding the rotor speed, compounded by the governor's permission to exceed the setpoint.
>
>
> The commanded ramp RPM held the stator at a higher frequency than the rotor, causing the observed slip. Closed-loop optical tracking without slip requires precise synchronization of stator angle with the rotor angle during acceleration. However, only one optical pulse per revolution is available, providing no feedback for the seven electrical cycles within that revolution. Between pulses, the firmware only knows the rotor completes one mechanical revolution in a period, $T_{rev}$. The challenge lies in accurately determining the stator frequency, $f_s$, to ensure the stator generates an appropriate number of electrical cycles for acceleration between pulses.
>
>
> The number of electrical cycles completed by the stator during one rotor revolution determines the change in the load angle, which relates the stator and rotor frequencies. The formula $N_s = 7 \cdot \frac{n_s}{n_r}$ shows this relationship, where $n_s$ is the desired speed, and $n_r$ is the actual rotor speed. The change in load angle per revolution, $\Delta\delta$, is given by $2520^\circ \times \frac{\Delta n}{n_r}$. This formula highlights how acceleration affects the load angle between electrical cycles.
>
>
> If rotor speed, $n_r$, lags the stator speed, $n_s$, by $\Delta n$, the load angle, $\delta$, increases each revolution by $\Delta\delta = 2520^\circ \times \frac{\Delta n}{n_r}$. If the rotor cannot accelerate, $\delta$ will slip past $180^\circ$ within a specific number of revolutions, entering the braking region.
>
> The rotor won't accelerate if the motor torque is less than the eddy brake torque ($\tau_{\text{motor}} < \tau_{\text{eddy}}$). When $\tau_{\text{motor}} > \tau_{\text{eddy}}$, the rotor accelerates, increasing $n_r$ and reducing the speed difference.

> The core issue is a fundamental misunderstanding of motor control in this FOC configuration. The system incorrectly attempts to drive the stator frequency higher than the rotor, believing this causes acceleration. In reality, the stator frequency *must* track the rotor, with acceleration achieved by increased voltage/current, generating torque exceeding drag. The code's attempt to offset the stator frequency from the rotor is fundamentally incorrect and prevents acceleration. This erroneous frequency offset introduces a relative rotation between the stator and the rotor.

> In a synchronous motor, increasing frequency *doesn't* pull it forward. Acceleration requires increasing the phase advance or voltage.
